title: Kestrel and the Terminal Again
premise: Marguerite Winterbourne, last navigator of the drifting fleet Kestrel, keeps the ancient beacon lit and avoids the hold where two thousand cryosleepers—her own earlier backups among them—wait for a decision no one alive is authorized to make. When a manifest anomaly surfaces a name that shouldn't exist, she discovers the fleet's founding truce expires in ninety days, forcing a choice between waking the original colonists or the backup generation. Through a fragile alliance with the anomaly's living descendant and the beacon's forgotten architect, Marguerite learns the truce was a lie built to hide a mutiny. In the end, she wakes neither half whole: she merges the manifests, sacrifices her own backups to power the revival, and steers the fleet toward an unclaimed world where both lineages land as one people.
about_author: Mara Hartwell is the pen name of a former maritime radio operator who spent a decade listening to beacons no one answered. She writes science fiction about inherited duties and the ghosts we keep operational.

chapters.title: The Light Nobody Ordered
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. On night watch aboard the Kestrel, she maintains the beacon whose commissioning records are missing, logging its pulse into a void that never answers. A routine supply run reveals a new name on the manifest of the Meridian, a ship that never flew: 'A. Voss.' The beat is quiet unease—the sense of being watched by paperwork.

chapters.title: Backups in the Hold
chapters.summary: Marguerite descends into the cryo hold against her habit, counting sleepers and finding one pod's registry scrubbed. Her POV establishes her guilt over her own stored backups and the fleet's unspoken rule: never wake what you can't account for. Emotional beat: dread dressed as diligence.

chapters.title: Ninety Days
chapters.summary: Council POV (via minutes Marguerite reads). The fleet's founding truce—a power-sharing pact between original crew lines and backup-generation descendants—expires in ninety days, and the council has quietly decided to let it lapse rather than choose. Marguerite realizes the beacon may be the truce's original failsafe. Beat: institutional cowardice.

chapters.title: A. Voss
chapters.summary: Marguerite traces the impossible name to Ilya Voss, a young hydroponics tech who claims never to have signed anything—and whose grandmother appears on the Meridian's crew list, decades dead. Their first meeting is wary, two people comparing scars of erasure. Beat: reluctant alliance.

chapters.title: The Ship That Never Flew
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. They board the dry-docked Meridian and find it fully provisioned for a voyage that logs say never happened, its navigation console keyed to the beacon's frequency. Someone intended to fly it during the mutiny era—and someone erased the flight. Beat: wonder curdling into conspiracy.

chapters.title: What the Beacon Remembers
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Deep in the beacon's core she finds analog memory drums: recordings of the founding generation, including a message from the beacon's architect, Ede Winterbourne—her grandmother—warning that the truce was designed to fail. Beat: inheritance as burden; family revealed as author of the trap.

chapters.title: Council of Small Mercies
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Marguerite and Ilya present findings to the council and are dismissed; worse, their access is revoked overnight. Ilya notices his grandmother's file has been altered since yesterday. Beat: the institution closing ranks, paranoia taking root.

chapters.title: The Mutiny Tapes
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. Decoding more drums, they hear the suppressed truth: the original crew tried to abandon the backups mid-voyage; loyalists scuttled the Meridian flight to stop them, and the truce froze both sides in place for generations. Beat: grief for ancestors who were neither heroes nor villains.

chapters.title: Cold Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The fleet's reactor can power waking only half the sleepers before systems degrade—one lineage lives, one stays frozen past recovery. She runs the numbers her grandmother left and finds Ede rigged them, weighting the outcome toward the backups. Beat: horror at being handed a pre-decided choice.

chapters.title: Sabotage at Third Watch
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. Someone vents coolant from the hold; forty pods drop to critical. Marguerite improvises a thermal bridge from the beacon itself, linking the light she tends to the lives she guards. Beat: crisis forging purpose; the beacon becomes a lifeline, not a relic.

chapters.title: The Loyalist's Daughter
chapters.summary: New POV: Councilor Ansel Rhee, descendant of the mutiny's losers, privately confesses he altered Ilya's file—not to destroy evidence but because his own family name is on the Meridian too. He offers the council's sealed archive. Beat: enemy becoming mirror; everyone is descended from both sides.

chapters.title: Sealed Archive
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. In the archive they find the truce's actual text: expiry triggers automatic revocation of navigation authority—which means whoever holds the beacon holds the fleet when day ninety arrives. Ede didn't just warn; she positioned her heirs. Beat: understanding the full scope of the inheritance.

chapters.title: Which Half Wakes
chapters.summary: Fleet-wide POV mosaic. Factions mobilize: original-line crews demand their elders wake first; backup-descendants refuse to be second-class survivors again. Marguerite, now publicly the beacon-keeper, becomes the symbol both sides court and threaten. Beat: rising tension, personal stakes going political.

chapters.title: Night of the Open Pods
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. Extremists force-open twelve pods as a demonstration; three sleepers die of shock. Marguerite broadcasts the mutiny tapes fleet-wide to reframe the conflict—not sides, but a shared crime and shared grief. Beat: tragedy forcing honesty; the middle path gets costly.

chapters.title: Ede's Last Entry
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The final memory drum contains Ede's confession: she scuttled the Meridian herself, and built the beacon so a future heir could choose better than she did—deliberately leaving the choice unrigged if the heir found this drum. The arithmetic Marguerite found was a test, not a verdict. Beat: forgiveness of the dead; agency reclaimed.

chapters.title: Truce Expires
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Day ninety arrives. The council dissolves per the treaty; command defaults to the beacon. Armed factions converge on the bridge while Marguerite stands at the nav console with sixty days of reactor margin and a plan nobody has approved. Beat: climax ignition—power arriving whether wanted or not.

chapters.title: The Third Manifest
chapters.summary: Climax part one. Under fire, Marguerite executes Ede's hidden protocol: merge the two lineage manifests into a single randomized roll, then sacrifice the backup pods' power cells—including her own—to triple the reactor output. Ilya holds the boarding parties at the hold doors, arguing, not fighting. Beat: self-sacrifice as thesis; inheritance given away, not kept.

chapters.title: Waking
chapters.summary: Climax part two, Marguerite's POV. The pods open across four days; the revived—originals and backups alike—wake to a fleet already transformed, greeted by descendants of both their betrayals and their loyalties. Marguerite watches her own younger backup step out and chooses not to meet her. Beat: awe, dislocation, mercy.

chapters.title: Course Correction
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. With the fleet united but resource-starved, the merged community ratifies a new compact and votes to leave the drift lanes for the unclaimed system the Meridian was originally bound for. Marguerite plots the course using the beacon as primary nav—the light finally answering someone. Beat: hope with labor attached.

chapters.title: Decommissioning the Ghosts
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She formally decommissions the empty pods, reads every name aloud over the beacon's frequency—an act of mourning broadcast to the fleet—and lets the Meridian be cannibalized for the crossing. Beat: ritual, grief metabolized into ceremony.

chapters.title: Landfall
chapters.summary: Fleet-wide mosaic POV. The Kestrel and her consorts enter orbit of the new world; first shuttles carry mixed crews deliberately, originals and backups side by side. Marguerite navigates the descent herself, the beacon's signal handed to a relay on the surface. Beat: arrival, belonging achieved rather than granted.

chapters.title: The Light Answers
chapters.summary: Marguerite's epilogue POV. Years later, she visits the surface relay where children who've never known the drift ask about the woman who kept the light. She tells them the truth: she didn't keep it alone, and it was never waiting for an answer—it was the answer. Final beat: memory as inheritance, belonging as a thing built and maintained daily.
